# webscour, full documentation

The seven documentation pages concatenated in reading order, for an agent that reads one file
instead of seven. Each section is preceded by the path of the page it came from. `llms.txt` is the
short entry point; this file is the bulk read.

Regenerate from the repository root. The header ends at the `<!-- pages -->` marker, and the loop
below rebuilds everything after it, so a rerun reproduces this file exactly:

```bash
sed -n '1,/^<!-- pages -->$/p' llms-full.txt > /tmp/lf
for p in index quickstart verbs sources privacy self-hosting contributing; do
  printf '\n---\n\n# docs/%s.md\n\n' "$p" >> /tmp/lf
  cat "docs/$p.md" >> /tmp/lf
done
mv /tmp/lf llms-full.txt
```

<!-- pages -->

# docs/index.md

# webscour

`webscour` is a Linux-first, dependency-free Python CLI that fetches the web for agents. The
executable is `wsc`. It searches the web through a local SearXNG first and falls back to
scrapers, queries GitHub, Stack Overflow, Hacker News, arXiv, Discourse and fourteen keyless API
endpoints directly, fetches a page as text or markdown, reads a PDF, maps a site from its
sitemap, and crawls a few pages politely. It renders with lightpanda, and playwright is the
fallback for a page that defeats lightpanda. It installs no Python package, needs no key and
opens no account.

It is not fast, and it does not claim to be. It is local, keyless, logless and terminal first:
one executable, text on stdout, failures on stderr, and an answer sized for an agent's context
instead of a browser tab.

**No key. No account. No log.**

```bash
wsc search "sqlite wal mode concurrent readers" --limit 5
wsc fetch https://example.com --max-chars 2000
wsc doctor
```

## Three ways in

The CLI is the source of truth. Two front ends call it rather than reimplementing it, and both
route their arguments through one mapping in `webscour/argv.py`, so a flag is added once and all
three stay in step.

| front end | how you reach it | what it is |
|---|---|---|
| CLI | `wsc <verb>` | the tool itself, documented on these pages |
| MCP server | `wsc mcp` | a stdio JSON-RPC server exposing one tool, `web_scour`, over the standard library only |
| pi tool | `extensions/pi/` | a pi extension that shells out to `wsc tool-argv` and runs the command it gets back |

`wsc tool-argv --json '{"action":"fetch","url":"https://example.com","max_chars":500}'` prints the
exact command line the other two front ends would run, which is the cheapest way to see what the
mapping does.

## The documentation

| page | read it for |
|---|---|
| [quickstart](quickstart.md) | install, run `wsc setup`, see real commands with their output, read what `wsc doctor` reports |
| [verbs](verbs.md) | every verb, its exact flags with defaults and types, an example, and the exit codes |
| [sources](sources.md) | the `--source` table, what each source queries, its rate limit, and how to choose one |
| [privacy](privacy.md) | exactly what leaves the machine, what never does, and how to verify the logging claim |
| [self-hosting](self-hosting.md) | what `wsc setup` writes, a different port, a remote SearXNG, clean removal |
| [contributing](contributing.md) | the module layout, the test command, the benchmark, the commit convention |

[routing.md](routing.md) is the cost and decision table for the source layer, [install.md](install.md)
covers the installer and the uninstall, and [maintaining.md](maintaining.md) is the release runbook.
The reasoning behind the five structural choices is in [decisions/](decisions/).

## Requirements, in one line each

Python 3.11 or newer. Linux, because `wsc setup` installs a systemd user unit. lightpanda on
`PATH` is required for rendering; `pdftotext`, `pandoc` and `markitdown` are optional and only
`wsc pdf` uses them. `wsc doctor` reports which of those it can see and ends in one verdict line.

Licence: MIT.

---

# docs/quickstart.md

# Quickstart

You need Python 3.11 or newer and Linux. The render path needs lightpanda on `PATH`; everything
else is optional.

## 1. Install

```bash
pipx install webscour                        # recommended: isolated venv, `wsc` on PATH
uvx webscour search "sqlite wal mode"        # no install at all, one run
uv tool install webscour                     # uv's managed tool environment
pip install --user webscour                  # plain pip, user prefix
```

From a checkout, with no build step:

```bash
cd webscour
python3 -m webscour.cli search "sqlite wal mode"
```

None of those install a Python dependency, because there are none. lightpanda is a system binary
and pip does not and should not manage it. Install it before you run anything that renders:

```bash
yay -S lightpanda-bin                                                        # Arch / AUR
curl -fsSL https://pkg.lightpanda.io/install.sh | bash -s "<version>"        # any Linux
brew install lightpanda-io/browser/lightpanda                                # Homebrew
```

`docs/install.md` has the full installer page, including the uninstall and the troubleshooting
checklist.

## 1b. Install the agent skill, if your agent reads one

The skill is what tells a model when to reach for `wsc` and which source to pick. It installs
separately from the tool, because a skill is read by the agent and the CLI is run by the shell:

```bash
pi install npm:webscour                       # pi, shortest form
npx skills add webscour                       # the open skills CLI
claude plugin marketplace add FurBlood344324/webscour   # Claude Code, then /plugin install webscour
```

With none of those, hand the agent the raw file:
`https://raw.githubusercontent.com/FurBlood344324/webscour/main/skill/SKILL.md`.

## 2. Install the search backend

```bash
wsc setup
```

That installs the bundled SearXNG: a shallow clone at a pinned commit, a venv, a generated
settings file, and one systemd user unit bound to `127.0.0.1:8888`. It also verifies that
lightpanda is on `PATH` and prints the install hint when it is not. The command is idempotent, so
a second run reports `unchanged` and restarts nothing.

`wsc setup` is a command you run, never a post-install hook. See [self-hosting](self-hosting.md)
for the paths it writes and how to remove them.

## 3. Check the machine

```bash
wsc doctor
```

`wsc doctor` reports in this order, and ends in one verdict line:

- `unit` is `active` and `enabled at boot`, because the systemd user unit is running.
- `listen` is `127.0.0.1:8888`, and nothing else. A non-loopback address is reported as
  `NOT loopback only` and degrades the verdict.
- `engines` is the number of engines the local instance loaded; `answered` is the subset that
  returned a row for one live probe query; `blocked` is SearXNG's own error table. Some engines
  are blocked from a residential IP, which is expected, not a fault.
- `backends` names lightpanda, playwright, pdftotext, pandoc and markitdown with `ok` or `no`.
- `render-venv` is either `absent` with the fix line, or the venv path with its health.
- `sources` lists the keyless endpoints and whether each is configured. `--live` probes them, at
  the cost of about a dozen requests, which is why it is not the default.

The verdict is one of `VERDICT OK`, `VERDICT DEGRADED: <reason>` or `VERDICT DOWN`. `OK` exits 0;
the other two exit 1, so a script can gate on it. Add `--json` for the same report as data.

```text
unit      active (enabled at boot)
listen    127.0.0.1:8888
engines   10 loaded
blocked   abcnyheter, brave, quark, yacy
answered  bing, mwmbl, naver, rawweb, seznam
silent    abcnyheter, brave, quark, wikibooks, yacy
backends  lightpanda=ok  playwright=no  pdftotext=ok  pandoc=ok  markitdown=ok
          playwright: not installed (only needed for a page lightpanda cannot render)
render-venv  absent (/home/<user>/.local/share/webscour/render-venv/bin/python)
             fallback only: wsc setup --playwright
sources   14 keyless endpoint(s)
          wikipedia    configured
          ...
VERDICT OK (5/10 engines answering, 4 blocked)
```

A blocked count above half of the loaded engines is `DEGRADED`, not `OK`. That threshold is
deliberate: a meta-search is expected to lose upstreams, a majority is not.

## 4. Three real commands

Search. Rows are numbered, the snippet is cut to 200 characters, and the bracket tag names the
upstream engines that produced the row:

```console
$ wsc search "sqlite wal mode concurrent readers" --limit 3
1. SQLite WAL Mode, and How LiteFS Replicates It · The Fly Blog - https://fly.io/blog/wal-mode-in-litefs/  [mwmbl,seznam]
   WAL Mode in LiteFS LiteFS is a distributed file system that magically replicates your SQLite databases. Make an update on one server and, voilà, your cha…
2. Introduce Sqlite WAL journal mode by lainedfles · Pull Request #… - https://github.com/evilsocket/opensnitch/pull/1011  [mwmbl]
   Saved searches Use saved searches to filter your results more quickly You signed in with another tab or window. Reload to refresh your session.You signed…
3. Write-Ahead Logging - https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html  [seznam]
   By default, SQLite does a checkpoint automatically when the WAL file reaches a threshold size of 1000 pages. (The Sqlite_Default_WAL_Autocheckpoint compile-time option can be used to specify a differ…
```

Fetch. Plain HTTP, no browser, and a cut marker when the text is longer than `--max-chars`:

```console
$ wsc fetch https://example.com --max-chars 120 --no-cache
This domain is for use in documentation examples without needing permission. This is not a service; avoid relying on it
... (cut at 120 chars)
```

Map. One URL per line, from the site's sitemap, a `Sitemap:` line in robots.txt, or llms.txt:

```console
$ wsc map https://docs.python.org --limit 4
https://docs.python.org/3.11/
https://docs.python.org/3.12/
https://docs.python.org/3.13/
https://docs.python.org/3.14/
```

Each of those writes its answer to stdout. When a render was unavoidable, stderr carries exactly
one extra line, `render: lightpanda` or `render: playwright`; a cache hit and a structured route
announce themselves the same way. Add `-v` to see why the tool chose what it chose.

## 5. If you are an agent

Two more entry points reach the same code without a shell in between:

```bash
wsc mcp         # a stdio JSON-RPC server with one tool, web_scour
wsc tool-argv --json '{"action":"fetch","url":"https://example.com"}'
```

The second prints the command line the MCP server and the pi extension both build, so what a
front end runs is inspectable. `--source web` is the default for all of them.

## 6. Where to go next

- [verbs](verbs.md) for every flag, its default and its type.
- [sources](sources.md) to query GitHub, Stack Overflow, Hacker News, arXiv, a Discourse forum or
  one of the keyless paper and package endpoints instead of the general web.
- [privacy](privacy.md) for what leaves the machine.

---

# docs/verbs.md

# Verbs

`wsc` has eleven verbs and one self-test. This page gives each its purpose, its exact flags with
defaults and types, one example, and its exit codes. Every flag below is read from the parser in
`webscour/cli.py`.

Before the verbs, the two rules that apply to all of them.

**stdout is the answer.** Search rows, page text, URL lists, crawl lines and the doctor table all
go to stdout. You can redirect stdout to a file and still have a usable page.

**stderr is silent by default.** It carries only what you need when the exit code is not 0, plus
three exceptions, which are facts about the answer rather than explanations: `render: <engine>`
when a browser produced the text, `cache: hit (<age>)` when the text came from the on-disk cache
instead of the network, and `route: <name>` when a site's own API answered. `-v` (or `--verbose`)
turns on the reasoning: which backend answered, why a page looked hollow, how long the pace slept,
which sitemap answered, which backend read a document. `search`, `setup`, `probe`, `cache` and
`pdf` take no `-v`; `fetch`, `map`, `crawl` and `doctor` do.

Exit codes in general: `0` success, `1` a verdict or a gate failed, `2` a usage error or a
backend that could not answer. argparse exits 2 on a missing positional, an unknown flag or an
invalid choice.

## search

One query, one page of results. `--source` selects the backend; `web` asks the local SearXNG
first and falls back to the DuckDuckGo lite page, the DuckDuckGo html page and Bing, in that
order. Rows print as `N. title - url  [engine,engine]` with the snippet indented below and cut to
200 characters.

| flag | type | default | meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `query` | positional, required | none | the search terms |
| `--source` | string | `web` | `web`, `github`, `so`, `hn`, `arxiv`, `discourse:<base>`, or a keyless API source |
| `--limit` | int | `8` | rows wanted; clamped to the range 1 to 30 |
| `--category` | choice | empty | a SearXNG category: `general`, `it`, `science`, `news`, `images`, `files`, `social`. Opt-in because a category changes which engines answer, so it changes the answer |
| `--fresh` | flag | off | the freshness rows only (Google News, BBC), sorted by publication date, newest first |
| `--since` | string, `YYYY-MM-DD` | empty | a date floor for `--fresh` |
| `--json` | flag | off | print an array of objects: `title`, `url`, `snippet`, `engines` |

`--source` also accepts the keyless endpoints `wikipedia`, `openalex`, `crossref`, `arxiv-api`,
`europepmc`, `pubmed`, `pypi`, `npm`, `crates`, `devto`, `wayback`, `googlenews` and `bbc`. See
[sources](sources.md).

```console
$ wsc search "sqlite wal mode concurrent readers" --limit 2
1. SQLite WAL Mode, and How LiteFS Replicates It · The Fly Blog - https://fly.io/blog/wal-mode-in-litefs/  [mwmbl,seznam]
   WAL Mode in LiteFS LiteFS is a distributed file system that magically replicates your SQLite databases. Make an update on one server and, voilà, your cha…
2. SQLite Forum: How does SQLite maintains state? - https://sqlite.org/forum/forumpost/f007a66e693f3c24?raw  [mwmbl]
   I was going through SQLite WAL mode and found the below statement in the docs >**3.1. Automatic Checkpoint** >By default, SQLite will automatically checkp…
```

With `--source github` the command makes two unauthenticated calls, repositories then issues, and
prints one extra stdout line at the end: `-- github rate limit remaining: <n>`.

Exit codes: `0` at least one row printed. `2` for an unknown `--source`, for zero results, and for
a usage error. A failed backend prints `backend <name>: <reason>` on stderr and the command moves
on to the next one; it exits 2 only when every backend failed or returned nothing.

## fetch

One URL as reading text. Plain HTTP by default: one request, HTML tokenized, navigation and
boilerplate dropped, blank lines removed. A page that is a JavaScript shell is retried once
through a render engine, and that retry is what prints `render: <engine>`.

| flag | type | default | meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `url` | positional, required | none | `http://` or `https://` |
| `--max-chars` | int | `6000` | cut the text here; a `... (cut at N chars)` line is appended |
| `--grep` | string, a regex | none | keep only matching lines, with one line of context and `>` on the match |
| `--format` | choice | `text` | `text` or `markdown`; markdown keeps headings, links and code fences |
| `--render` | flag | off | force a browser; no silent fallback if none is usable |
| `--render-engine` | choice | `auto` | `lightpanda`, `playwright` or `auto`, which tries lightpanda first |
| `--archive` | flag | off | force the Wayback Machine snapshot; a live page that answers 404 or 410 already does this |
| `--no-route` | flag | off | ignore the structured per-site routes and always take the plain path |
| `--save` | flag | off | also write the page into `./.webscour/` |
| `--save-only` | flag | off | write it and print one index line instead of the page |
| `--fresh` | flag | off | ignore the cache for this call; the network is read |
| `--ttl` | string duration | empty (24h) | cache freshness window, for example `30m` or `7d` |
| `--no-cache` | flag | off | neither read nor write the cache |
| `--max-size` | int | `5242880` | the largest page, in bytes, that `--save` will write |
| `-v`, `--verbose` | flag | off | explain every choice on stderr |

```console
$ wsc fetch https://example.com --max-chars 120 --no-cache
This domain is for use in documentation examples without needing permission. This is not a service; avoid relying on it
... (cut at 120 chars)
```

```console
$ wsc fetch https://example.com --grep "documentation" --no-cache
> This domain is for use in documentation examples without needing permission. This is not a service; avoid relying on it for testing and monitoring purposes.
```

A PDF or docx URL is routed through the same local extractors `pdf` uses. A forum topic URL on
`forums.developer.nvidia.com` is read through its `.json` form, which needs no render.

Exit codes: `0` text printed. `1` `--grep` was given and no line matched; the text was not
printed. `2` the fetch failed (HTTP error, DNS failure, empty document), the text was empty, or
`--grep` was not a valid regex. `--render` with no usable engine exits 2 and names every engine it
tried.

## pdf

A paper or a manual as text, from a URL or a local file. The first working local backend reads it:
`pdftotext` then `markitdown` for a PDF, `pandoc` then `markitdown` for docx and epub. Nothing is
uploaded and no service is involved.

| flag | type | default | meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `source` | positional, required | none | an `http(s)` URL or a path on disk |
| `--max-chars` | int | `20000` | cut the text here, with the same cut marker as `fetch` |
| `--format` | choice | `text` | `text` or `markdown`; only pandoc can produce markdown, so a PDF stays plain either way |
| `-v`, `--verbose` | flag | off | name the format and the backend that produced the text |

```console
$ wsc pdf https://arxiv.org/pdf/1706.03762 --max-chars 200
                                            Provided proper attribution is provided, Google hereby grants permission to
                                            reproduce the tables and figures in
… (cut at 200 chars)
```

Exit codes: `0` text printed. `2` the path does not exist, the URL is not a document, no backend
could read the format, or the document has no text layer (a scan). The last case says so on
stderr and stops; OCR is out of scope.

## map

The URL list for a site. It asks four candidate documents in order, the cheapest first:
`/sitemap.xml`, `/sitemap_index.xml`, the `Sitemap:` line in `/robots.txt`, then `/llms.txt`. It
prints the first one that answers.

| flag | type | default | meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `url` | positional, required | none | any URL on the site; only scheme and host are used |
| `--limit` | int | `200` | stop after this many URLs; below 1 is raised to 1 |
| `-v`, `--verbose` | flag | off | name the document that answered and how many URLs were withheld |

```console
$ wsc map https://docs.python.org --limit 4
https://docs.python.org/3.11/
https://docs.python.org/3.12/
https://docs.python.org/3.13/
https://docs.python.org/3.14/
```

Exit codes: `0` at least one URL printed. `2` none of the four candidates answered, with
`map: no sitemap, robots Sitemap line or llms.txt answered at <origin>` on stderr.

## crawl

A short polite crawl. It seeds from `map`, then follows same-origin links breadth first, and
prints one line per page: `url  |  title  |  N chars`. It writes nothing to disk.

| flag | type | default | meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `url` | positional, required | none | the seed URL |
| `--depth` | int | `1` | link depth; below 0 is raised to 0, and 0 fetches the seed only |
| `--limit` | int | `20` | maximum pages fetched; clamped to the range 1 to 200 |
| `--same-origin` | flag | on | stay on the seed origin; this is the default |
| `--any-origin` | flag | off | leave the origin; mutually exclusive with `--same-origin` |
| `-v`, `--verbose` | flag | off | report the page count, the depth, the origin rule and the pacing |

```console
$ wsc crawl https://example.com --limit 3
https://example.com  |  Example Domain  |  156 chars
```

Every request in a crawl waits so that two live fetches stay at least one second apart, and the
stamp is shared across processes. A crawl of N pages therefore takes at least N seconds.

Exit codes: `0` at least one page printed. `2` nothing was fetched.

## cache

Four verbs over the on-disk cache, which is `<cwd>/.webscour/`: one markdown file per fetched URL
and an index beside them. Reading is on by default with a 24 hour window; writing only happens
when `fetch` was given `--save`, `--save-only`, or when `cache get` misses.

| flag | type | default | meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `action` | positional, required | none | `list`, `get <url>`, `prune`, or `path` |
| `url` | positional, optional | none | required by `get` |
| `--older-than` | string duration | `7d` | the prune window |
| `--all` | flag | off | `prune` only: remove the whole directory |
| `--json` | flag | off | print the index as one JSON object |

```console
$ wsc cache list
fetched                 bytes      age format     file
2026-11-15 00:08:34       157       2s markdown   0f115db0-example-com.md
1 entry, 157 bytes, /home/<user>/.webscour
```

`cache get <url>` returns the cached text, and on a miss it fetches the page, saves it and prints
it. It ignores the TTL on purpose: asking for a specific URL means you want that file. `cache path`
prints the directory. `cache prune` reports every file it removed and the bytes freed.

Exit codes: `0` for `list`, `path`, a successful `prune`, and a `get` that answered. `2` for a
`get` with no URL, a bad action (argparse), an unreadable index, or a `get` whose fetch failed.

## doctor

The health check. It reports the systemd user unit, the listener, the loaded engine count, which
engines are blocked in SearXNG's own error table, which engines answered one live probe query,
which engines are silent, the render and document backends, the render venv, the keyless sources,
and one verdict line. It changes nothing.

| flag | type | default | meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--json` | flag | off | print the same report as one JSON object after the table |
| `--live` | flag | off | probe every keyless endpoint once; a dozen requests, so it is not the default |
| `-v`, `--verbose` | flag | off | name which source failed and why, on stderr |

```console
$ wsc doctor
unit      active (enabled at boot)
listen    127.0.0.1:8888
engines   10 loaded
blocked   abcnyheter, brave, quark, yacy
answered  bing, mwmbl, naver, rawweb, seznam
silent    abcnyheter, brave, quark, wikibooks, yacy
backends  lightpanda=ok  playwright=no  pdftotext=ok  pandoc=ok  markitdown=ok
          playwright: not installed (only needed for a page lightpanda cannot render)
render-venv  absent (/home/<user>/.local/share/webscour/render-venv/bin/python)
             fallback only: wsc setup --playwright
sources   14 keyless endpoint(s)
          wikipedia    configured
          ...
VERDICT OK (5/10 engines answering, 4 blocked)
```

The verdict has three forms. `VERDICT DOWN` when nothing is listening or no engine answered.
`VERDICT DEGRADED: <reason>` when lightpanda is missing, when the listener is not loopback only,
or when more than half of the loaded engines are blocked. `VERDICT OK (<n>/<m> engines answering,
<k> blocked)` otherwise.

Exit codes: `0` for `OK`. `1` for `DOWN` and for `DEGRADED`. A script can gate on the exit code
alone and read nothing.

## setup

The installer. Bare `wsc setup` means "install the local SearXNG"; the render fallback is a
separate install and needs its own flag, because a search backend and a browser are two different
capabilities. It is idempotent: a second run reports `unchanged` and restarts nothing.

| flag | type | default | meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--searxng` | flag | off | install the local SearXNG user unit; bare `setup` does this too |
| `--playwright` | flag | off | install the render fallback into `~/.local/share/webscour/render-venv` |
| `--all` | flag | off | both installs in one run |
| `--with-deps` | flag | off | let playwright install chromium's OS packages; needs root |
| `--force` | flag | off | rebuild what is already there |
| `--no-start` | flag | off | install without starting the unit |
| `--check` | flag | off | report state and change nothing |

```console
$ wsc setup --check
src            de722ab
venv           present
settings       1938
state          present
unit           enabled / active
listen         127.0.0.1:8888
lightpanda  /usr/bin/lightpanda
```

Exit codes: `0` everything asked for is in place. `1` lightpanda is not on `PATH` after a SearXNG
install, or the playwright install failed; both print the exact fix. The SearXNG step returns the
bundled installer's own exit code, which is `2` for an unknown option and `1` for a failed
preflight.

## probe

The engine measurement. It asks the local SearXNG a fixed query set and reports, per engine, the
success rate, the median latency, whether the page was a bot check and its category. `--quality`
is the wider measurement that decides which engines are worth keeping.

| flag | type | default | meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--engines` | string, comma separated | all candidates | measure only these engines |
| `--quality` | flag | off | the 30-query coverage and precision measurement |
| `--write` | flag | off | with `--quality`, write the survivors to the engine state file |
| `--json` | flag | off | print the rows as JSON |

```console
$ wsc probe --engines naver,bing
 1/2 naver          100.0%  median 0.83s  blocked 0  general web
 2/2 bing            40.0%  median 0.18s  blocked 0  general web

keep (>=70% success, no block, web category): naver
```

`--write` only stores a set the measurement kept: an empty result is refused and the settings are
left untouched. The file it writes is not live until the installer renders it again, and the
command prints that reminder.

Exit codes: `0` the measurement ran. `1` the local SearXNG did not answer, or `--write` had an
empty set to store. `2` an unknown option reached the bundled script.

## mcp

A stdio JSON-RPC server that exposes one tool, `web_scour`, over the standard library only. It is
a front end, not a second implementation: it builds an argv with `webscour/argv.py` and runs the
same commands you would type.

| flag | type | default | meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| none | | | it speaks JSON-RPC on stdin and stdout |

```console
$ wsc mcp
```

Exit codes: `0` the client closed the stream. `2` no server file was found, which happens in a
wheel that does not ship one; the message names the three paths it looked in.

## tool-argv

The mapping itself, for a front end that is not Python. It takes one JSON object of tool
parameters and prints the argv, the error if there was one, and the command line as you would
type it.

| flag | type | default | meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--json` | string, JSON | none; stdin is read when absent | one tool call: `{"action": ..., "query" or "url": ..., ...}` |

```console
$ wsc tool-argv --json '{"action":"fetch","url":"https://example.com","max_chars":500}'
{"argv": ["fetch", "https://example.com", "--max-chars", "500"], "error": "", "command": "wsc fetch https://example.com --max-chars 500"}
```

The action is one of `search`, `fetch`, `pdf`, `map` or `crawl`. `build` never raises: an
unusable call comes back with a non-empty `error` and an empty `argv`, which is why a front end
does not need a try/except to stay quiet.

Exit codes: `0` a usable argv. `2` invalid JSON, or a call the mapping refused.

## The entry points

`wsc` is a console script that calls one function, `webscour.cli:main`. Four spellings reach that
function and the same exit code.

- `wsc <verb>` is the console script, installed by pipx, uv or pip.
- `python3 -m webscour` and `python3 -m webscour.cli` run `main()` in process. Use these from a
  checkout with no build step, and in a test that must not depend on `PATH`. The module entry
  point also maps `Ctrl-C` to exit 130 and a closed stdout pipe to exit 0.
- `web` is the name the tool had before it was published. Where a local wrapper for it exists it
  `exec`s `wsc` rather than reimplementing anything, so an old habit or an old script reaches the
  same code. That wrapper lives outside this repository and is not installed by the package.

## `--self-test`

```console
$ wsc --self-test
PASS ddg lite parser
...
SUMMARY pass=30 fail=0
```

Thirty checks of the pure parts: the result parsers, the source parsers, the extraction rules, the
markdown conformance suite, the document router, the sitemap reader, the origin filter, the
js-shell heuristic and the no-identity check. It runs offline with no SearXNG and no render
backend, which is why `scripts/check.sh` uses it as a gate. Exit code `0` when every check passed,
`1` otherwise.

## Global flags

| flag | meaning |
|---|---|
| `-h`, `--help` | print the usage block and exit 0 |
| `-V`, `--version` | print `webscour <version>` and exit 0 |
| `--self-test` | run the offline checks |

`wsc` with no arguments prints the same usage block and exits `1`, so an empty invocation is not
mistaken for success. An unknown verb prints `unknown command '<name>'` on stderr, the usage block
on stdout, and exits `2`.

---

# docs/sources.md

# Sources

`--source` decides who gets asked. Every source is keyless: no API token, no account and no
client id sits anywhere in this tool. Rate limits are the ones the upstream service publishes or
enforces, so they are properties of your IP, not of this tool.

## The three families

The source layer has three shapes, and the shape tells you what to expect.

- **The local meta-search**, `web`. One loopback call, several upstream engines merged, and each
  row tagged with the engines that produced it. This is the general case.
- **Direct service APIs**, `github`, `so`, `hn`, `arxiv` and `discourse:<base>`. One named
  service, its own ranking, its own rate limit.
- **Keyless single-purpose endpoints**, the fourteen below. One endpoint per kind of question,
  each with a pure parser that `--self-test` exercises offline.

`docs/routing.md` carries the decision table and the measured cost of each family.

## The table

| `--source` | what it queries | key | rate limit | output shape |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `web` (default) | the local SearXNG on `http://127.0.0.1:8888`, which fans out to its enabled engines; then the DuckDuckGo lite page, the DuckDuckGo html page and Bing | none | SearXNG's engines pace themselves; the CLI spaces live queries to at most one per second across processes | rows tagged with their engines, `[naver,bing]` |
| `github` | `api.github.com/search/repositories` and `api.github.com/search/issues` | none | 10 requests per minute unauthenticated; one `github` search spends 2 of them | repo rows carry language and stars; issue rows carry state and body |
| `so` | `api.stackexchange.com/2.3/search/advanced` with `site=stackoverflow` | none | Stack Exchange's anonymous quota; the command reports a refusal, it does not retry | `title (score N)`, then `answered` or `open` plus tags |
| `hn` | `hn.algolia.com/api/v1/search` | none | Algolia's public search tier; no batch mode here | `title`, then points and comment count |
| `arxiv` | `export.arxiv.org/api/query`, the Atom feed | none | arXiv's request policy; one query per call | `title`, the `abs` URL, the abstract as the snippet |
| `discourse:<base>` | `<base>/search.json?q=<query>` | none | the forum's own anonymous limit | topic title, topic URL, blurb |
| `wikipedia` | `en.wikipedia.org/w/api.php`, list=search | none | none published; one request per call | article title and the article URL |
| `openalex` | `api.openalex.org/works` | none | none published; a polite email pool exists but this tool sends no identity | work title, DOI or landing URL, abstract |
| `crossref` | `api.crossref.org/works` | none | none published | work title, DOI URL, container and year |
| `arxiv-api` | the same Atom endpoint as `arxiv`, under the alias the tool-call schema uses | none | as `arxiv` | as `arxiv` |
| `europepmc` | `ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search` | none | none published | title, DOI, PubMed or Europe PMC URL |
| `pubmed` | `eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi` | none | NCBI's policy; a keyless call gets the default pool | title, PubMed URL, journal and date |
| `pypi` | `pypi.org/pypi/<name>/json` | none | none published | project name, PyPI URL, version, summary, release date |
| `npm` | `registry.npmjs.org/<name>/latest` | none | none published | package name, npm URL, version, description |
| `crates` | `crates.io/api/v1/crates/<name>` | none | crates.io asks for a descriptive user agent, which the tool sends | crate name, crates.io URL, version, description |
| `devto` | `dev.to/api/articles?tag=<tag>` | none | dev.to's public limit | article title, URL, tags, reactions |
| `wayback` | `web.archive.org/cdx/search/cdx` | none | the archive rate-limits bursts; a 429 is reported as a note, not a failure | snapshot URL and timestamp |
| `googlenews` | `news.google.com/rss/search` | none | Google's RSS limits; no key involved | headline, source, publication date |
| `bbc` | `feeds.bbci.co.uk/news/rss.xml` | none | none published; one feed read per call | headline, article URL, date |

`<base>` is a full origin with a scheme, for example
`discourse:https://forums.developer.nvidia.com`. A `--source` value that matches none of those
shapes is a usage error: stderr lists every accepted value and the exit code is 2.

`--fresh` is not a source. It restricts the answer to the freshness rows (Google News, BBC and
SearXNG's news category), merges them, and sorts by publication date with the newest first.
`--since YYYY-MM-DD` sets the floor for that sort.

## What each source is good at

**`web`.** The default, and the right first attempt for a question about the world. The local
SearXNG merges several upstream engines, so one suspended engine does not empty the answer, and
each row tells you which engines produced it. When the local service is down the command falls
back to the three scrapers, one `backend <name>: <reason>` line per attempt on stderr. From a
residential IP those scrapers mostly answer a bot check, so the local backend is the one that
matters.

**`github`.** Code, not prose. Use it when the answer is a repository (a library that does X) or
an issue (someone already hit this error). It spends two API calls per query and prints the
remaining budget, so a loop is easy to stay under.

**`so`.** A symptom, an error text, a stack trace. Stack Overflow rows carry the score and
whether the question is answered, which is the cheapest signal about whether the page will help.
Prefer it over `web` when your query is an exception message rather than a concept.

**`hn`.** Opinion and experience: "has anyone run this in production", "what did people say about
this release". Story points and comment counts are the ranking you actually get, so a low-score
row is not worth opening.

**`arxiv`.** A paper, by topic rather than by citation. The snippet is the abstract, so one query
often decides whether you need the PDF; follow up with `wsc pdf` on the `abs` URL's `/pdf/` form.
Prefer it over `web` for anything where a blog summary would be second hand.

**`discourse:<base>`.** One forum's own search, which is the only way to reach posts that no
general engine indexes. The NVIDIA developer forum is the worked example; the same shape works
for any Discourse instance that leaves anonymous search on.

**The scholarly four** (`openalex`, `crossref`, `europepmc`, `pubmed`). Use them when you want a
record rather than prose: a DOI, a citation, a journal, a date. `pubmed` and `europepmc` overlap
by design and differ in what they index; `openalex` is the widest net and `crossref` is the
metadata of record for a DOI.

**The package four** (`pypi`, `npm`, `crates`, `devto`). These are exact lookups by name, not
searches. `wsc search requests --source pypi` either finds the project or does not; it is a check,
not a query.

**`wayback`, `googlenews`, `bbc`.** `wayback` answers "what did this URL say before it died", and
`fetch --archive` uses the same machinery. `googlenews` and `bbc` are the freshness pair: the
answer is a dated headline, and `--fresh` is how you get them sorted.

## Choosing a source

1. Is the answer a paper? Use `arxiv`, or `openalex` / `crossref` / `pubmed` if you want a DOI and
   a citation record rather than an abstract.
2. Is the answer a repository or an issue? Use `github`.
3. Is the query an error message or a stack trace? Use `so`.
4. Do you want experience rather than documentation? Use `hn`.
5. Do you want a package's current version? Use `pypi`, `npm` or `crates`.
6. Is the question specific to a product whose forum you know? Use `discourse:<base>`.
7. Do you need something published in the last day? Use `--fresh`, or `googlenews` / `bbc`
   directly.
8. Do you need a page that no longer exists? Use `wayback`, or `fetch --archive`.
9. Otherwise use `web`. It is the default because it is the general case, and its rows tell you
   which engine answered so a bad answer is diagnosable.

Two habits worth keeping:

- Run `web` first when you do not know which of the others applies. The rows name their engines,
  and a specialised source can be the second query rather than a guess.
- `github`, `so`, the package four and `discourse` are exact-match searches over a small corpus. A
  natural-language question does badly there; three or four distinctive words do well.

## Forums and documents

`fetch` rewrites a topic URL on `forums.developer.nvidia.com` to the thread's `.json` form and
prints `#post author` with plain text. That is the readable version of a forum page and it needs
no render.

`fetch` also resolves a known site through its own API when the plain page is measurably worse,
and announces it on stderr as `route: <name>`. `--no-route` turns that off. A route that declines
falls back to the plain path and says so only under `-v`; a route never turns a page that used to
work into a failure.

`pdf` and `fetch` share one document path: a URL whose content type or extension is a PDF, docx or
epub is downloaded once and handed to the first working local backend. Nothing is uploaded
anywhere to read it.

---

# docs/privacy.md

# Privacy

This page states what leaves the machine, what does not, what is logged, and how to check the
claims yourself. Everything here describes the default configuration: the bundled local SearXNG
on loopback, and nothing else. If you point the CLI at a remote SearXNG you have changed the
trust boundary, and the last section says what that means.

## What leaves the machine

Exactly one thing for a search: **the query**.

1. `wsc search "<query>"` sends the query text to `http://127.0.0.1:8888`, the local SearXNG,
   over loopback. That request also carries `format=json`, `safesearch=0` and `timeout_limit=6`.
2. SearXNG forwards the query to whichever of its enabled upstream engines your IP can use. That
   is the only step where the query leaves the machine, and it is SearXNG doing it, not this CLI.
3. `wsc fetch`, `wsc map` and `wsc crawl` send the URL you named, and nothing else, to the host
   that URL points at. There is no query in those requests.
4. `wsc search --source <service>` skips SearXNG and sends the query straight to that service.
   That is one service, named in the command, instead of a meta-search.

The outgoing request headers are fixed and minimal: one user agent string identifying a normal
browser, `Accept-Language: en-US,en;q=0.9`, and the accept header the request needs. There is no
cookie jar, no referrer, no client id, and no header carrying anything about you.

`wsc --self-test` is the exception that proves the rule: it opens no socket at all. It runs
offline by construction, and `scripts/check.sh` depends on that.

## What never leaves

None of these are read by the tool, so none of them can be sent:

- **URLs you fetch.** `map` and `crawl` send only the URL you gave them, plus the links they
  follow on that same origin. Nothing about what you fetched goes anywhere else.
- **Your working directory.** The tool never asks the process for it in order to identify you.
  Its cache directory is resolved relative to the working directory for a local file write only,
  and that path is never sent.
- **Your hostname.** No `gethostname` call exists in the code.
- **Your username and home path.** The tool resolves its own directories by expanding `~`,
  locally only. Nothing sends the result.
- **Your project names.** Nothing enumerates a project, a repository or a config file in your
  working tree.

That is not an assurance to take on faith. `wsc --self-test` includes a check named
`no identity in request` that reads the source of `webscour/cli.py` and fails if the assembly
`get` + `pass`, `gethost` + `name` or `get` + `login` appears anywhere in it. Those three are the
ways a Python program reads the pieces of an identity, and the check is why they are absent rather
than merely unused.

## What is logged

**The tool logs nothing.** It writes no log file, no history and no state about your queries. Two
files it does write are yours and local:

- `~/.cache/web/last-live` holds one floating point timestamp of the last live request, which is
  what enforces at most one web query per second across processes. It holds a number, not a
  query, and `cat` shows it.
- `./.webscour/` exists only if you asked for it with `--save`, `--save-only` or `cache get`. It
  contains the page text you asked to keep and an index beside it. `wsc cache path` prints the
  directory and `wsc cache prune --all` removes it.

**The bundled SearXNG drops the query.** Stock SearXNG logs the outgoing request URL at WARNING
from `searx.network.<engine>`, and that URL carries the query text as `?q=...`. The bundled unit
does three things about that:

- `GRANIAN_LOG_ACCESS_ENABLED=false` in the unit, so there is no access log at all.
- `GRANIAN_LOG_LEVEL=warning`, so nothing below a warning is emitted.
- `searx/serve.py` is the WSGI entrypoint instead of stock `searx.webapp`, and it installs a
  `logging.Filter` on the root logger, `searx`, `searx.network`, `searx.search`, `searx.webapp`
  and `granian`. The filter rewrites every URL query string in a record to `?<query withheld>`
  before any handler sees the record, keeping the host so the warning still says which engine was
  suspended.

Autocomplete is off in the generated settings (`autocomplete: ""`), so no keystroke leaves the
box. `query_in_title` is off. Metrics are on, because `/stats/errors` is what `wsc doctor` reads,
and that endpoint carries engine failure counts and no query text.

## How to verify it

Read the three files that make the claim. They are short and they are the actual mechanism.

```bash
sed -n '1,43p' searx/serve.py        # the filter, and the loggers it is installed on
sed -n '199,231p' searx/install.sh   # the unit: bind, access log, level, entrypoint
sed -n '128,164p' searx/install.sh   # the generated settings: autocomplete, metrics, bind
```

Then check the running machine rather than the source:

```bash
systemctl --user cat searxng-local        # the installed unit, with its environment
ss -ltn | grep 8888                       # one row, and it starts 127.0.0.1:
journalctl --user -u searxng-local -n 50  # recent records; no query text in any of them
```

Run a query you can recognise, then read the journal:

```bash
wsc search "privacy-check-marker-<a word you never use>" --limit 1
journalctl --user -u searxng-local --since "2 min ago"
```

You will see the engine warnings, if any, with `?<query withheld>` where a URL would have carried
your terms, and no record containing the marker. That is the whole claim, and it is falsifiable in
two commands.

To check what actually leaves your machine to the internet rather than to loopback, watch the
sockets:

```bash
ss -tunp | grep -i searx                  # the SearXNG process's outbound connections
```

Those connections go to the upstream engines, and they carry the query. That is what a
meta-search does.

## Where the tool sits, and where it does not protect you

- **Your IP is your identity to the upstream engines.** A local proxy does not change that. The
  point of the local SearXNG is that no third party sees who is asking through an API key, not
  that the request is anonymous.
- **Send generic technical terms.** Private context in a query is a mistake regardless of the log
  settings, because the upstream engine receives the query by design.
- **A direct `--source` is a direct request.** A service named on the command line sees the query
  and your IP, from your machine, with no middleman. Those services keep their own logs, and this
  tool has no say in that.
- **`fetch`, `map` and `crawl` reveal the URL to that site.** A crawl of a private intranet host
  is visible to that host. The tool paces requests but does not hide them.

## If you point it at a remote SearXNG

The CLI reads one environment variable for the backend:

```bash
export WEBSEARCH_SEARXNG="https://searx.example.net"
wsc search "sqlite wal mode"
```

That changes the trust boundary completely, and you should be explicit about how:

- **The query travels over the network to that host** before it reaches any engine, so the
  operator of that instance sees it, and so does every hop in between unless the URL is https.
- **The log claim stops applying.** `searx/serve.py` and the generated settings belong to the
  bundled unit on your machine. A remote instance runs whatever its operator installed.
- **`wsc doctor` reports on that host, not on yours.** It will call a remote instance healthy and
  endorse it, because health is all it measures.

The default is loopback, and the reason to keep it there is that it is the only configuration in
which every claim on this page is a property of code you can read on your own disk.

Related: [self-hosting](self-hosting.md) covers what `wsc setup` writes and how to remove it, and
[sources](sources.md) names the services a direct `--source` query reaches.

---

# docs/self-hosting.md

# Self-hosting the search backend

`wsc setup` installs one thing: a SearXNG instance that belongs to your user, listens on
loopback, and exists so that `wsc search --source web` has somewhere local to ask. This page says
exactly what that install touches, how to move it to another port, how to use a remote instance
instead, and how to remove it so nothing is left behind.

You can read the installer instead of trusting this page: it is `searx/install.sh`, 267 lines,
and it is the only thing `wsc setup` runs. `wsc setup` shells out to it rather than reimplementing
it, so there is one definition of "installed".

## What `wsc setup` writes

Everything below is under your home directory, and all of it is yours. No sudo is used and no
system-wide path is touched. The installer refuses to run as root for exactly that reason.

| path | what it is |
|---|---|
| `~/.local/share/searxng/src` | a shallow git clone of SearXNG, checked out detached at a pinned commit (`de722ab1bc95`, SearXNG 1.0.0). A commit, not a tag, because a tag can move |
| `~/.local/share/searxng/venv` | a Python venv made with `python3.11` (override with `SEARX_PYTHON`), with `requirements.txt` and `requirements-server.txt` installed. It provides `granian`, the WSGI server the unit runs |
| `~/.local/share/searxng/venv/.searx-install` | a marker holding the commit and a hash of the requirements. When it matches, pip is skipped, which is what makes a second install fast |
| `~/.local/share/searxng/engines.json` | the engine state. Absent means every candidate is enabled. `wsc probe --quality --write` writes it, and the next install renders it into the settings |
| `~/.local/share/searxng/serve.py` | a copy of `searx/serve.py`, the WSGI entrypoint with the query-redacting log filter. It is copied here so the unit never reads a repository |
| `~/.config/searxng/secret_key` | 48 bytes of `secrets.token_urlsafe`, mode 600, generated once and kept across rebuilds so the settings do not churn |
| `~/.config/searxng/settings.yml` | the generated settings, mode 600. Never hand-edit it: the installer rewrites it from `engines.json` on the next run |
| `~/.config/systemd/user/searxng-local.service` | the systemd **user** unit, mode 644 |

The unit runs as your user, in your user session, and is enabled so it starts at login. Its
service section is deliberately narrow. It sets `SEARXNG_SETTINGS_PATH`, `GRANIAN_INTERFACE=wsgi`,
`GRANIAN_HOST=127.0.0.1`, `GRANIAN_PORT=8888`, `GRANIAN_LOG_LEVEL=warning`,
`GRANIAN_LOG_ACCESS_ENABLED=false` and `ExecStart=<venv>/bin/granian serve:app`, plus
`NoNewPrivileges=yes`, `PrivateTmp=yes`, `ProtectSystem=strict`, `ProtectHome=read-only` and
`ReadWritePaths` limited to `~/.local/share/searxng`.

The generated settings pin the parts that matter: `server.bind_address: 127.0.0.1`,
`limiter: false`, `public_instance: false`, `image_proxy: false`, `autocomplete: ""`,
`query_in_title: false`, `enable_metrics: true`, `outgoing.request_timeout: 4.0` and
`outgoing.max_request_timeout: 6.0`. Appended to that are the engine list and a per-engine
timeout.

After writing, the installer enables the unit, restarts it when anything changed, and waits for
the port to answer. A second run with nothing changed prints `unchanged` through its steps and
leaves the running service alone.

## Check it, without changing anything

```console
$ wsc setup --check
src            de722ab
venv           present
settings       1938
state          present
unit           enabled / active
listen         127.0.0.1:8888
lightpanda  /usr/bin/lightpanda
```

`src` is the short commit, `settings` is the file size in bytes, `state` says whether an engine
selection exists, and `lightpanda` is the path the render path will use or a warning that it is
not on `PATH`. `--check` exits 0 without writing anything.

For the operational view, which includes engine health and one verdict line:

```bash
wsc doctor
wsc doctor --json
```

## Run it on a different port

There is no `--port` flag. The port is written in two places, and both are generated, so the
honest procedure is to change both and then not re-run the installer until you mean to (the
installer rewrites them from its own hardcoded `8888`).

1. Stop the unit:

   ```bash
   systemctl --user stop searxng-local
   ```

2. Change the port in the settings file, in the `server:` section:

   ```yaml
   server:
     bind_address: "127.0.0.1"
     port: 8899
   ```

3. Change the port the unit passes to granian, with a drop-in rather than an edit:

   ```bash
   systemctl --user edit searxng-local
   ```

   In the override:

   ```ini
   [Service]
   Environment=GRANIAN_PORT=8899
   ```

   A drop-in is the right tool here precisely because `install.sh` rewrites the unit file itself;
   an override survives that rewrite.

4. Reload, start, and confirm:

   ```bash
   systemctl --user daemon-reload
   systemctl --user start searxng-local
   ss -ltn | grep 8899
   ```

5. Point the CLI at it. The backend address comes from one environment variable:

   ```bash
   export WEBSEARCH_SEARXNG="http://127.0.0.1:8899"
   wsc search "sqlite wal mode" --limit 3
   ```

   Put that export in your shell profile if the port is permanent. `wsc doctor` reads the same
   variable, so it checks the port you actually use.

`wsc setup --check` keeps checking `8888`, because that is the bundled installer's own view of the
world. Use `wsc doctor` for the truth about a moved instance.

## Use a remote SearXNG instead

If you already run a SearXNG elsewhere, or you trust an instance someone else runs, do not install
the bundled one. Set the same variable:

```bash
export WEBSEARCH_SEARXNG="https://searx.example.net"
wsc search "postgres index bloat" --limit 5
```

The variable is read once, at import time, and trailing slashes are stripped. Everything that
talks to the search backend uses it: `search --source web`, `doctor`, and the start-if-stopped
attempt. Against a remote instance the start attempt is harmless: it only tries
`systemctl --user start searxng-local` when the port refuses, and moves on when that fails.

Read [privacy](privacy.md) before you do this. A remote instance changes who sees your query, and
the log redaction this project installs applies only to the unit it installs.

## Remove it cleanly

There is no `wsc uninstall`. The pieces are named, so removal is four commands.

```bash
systemctl --user disable --now searxng-local
rm -f ~/.config/systemd/user/searxng-local.service
systemctl --user daemon-reload
rm -rf ~/.local/share/searxng ~/.config/searxng
```

What that does, in order: stops the service and removes it from the boot set; deletes the unit
file; reloads systemd so the unit is forgotten; then deletes the clone, the venv, the copied
`serve.py`, the engine state, the generated settings and the secret.

Two things it deliberately does not touch:

- `~/.cache/web/last-live`, the one-second pacing stamp. It holds a timestamp, no query, and it
  is harmless; `rm -rf ~/.cache/web` if you want it gone.
- The `wsc` executable and the Python package. Removing those is your package manager's job:
  `pipx uninstall webscour`, `uv tool uninstall webscour`, or `pip uninstall webscour`.

After removal, `wsc search --source web` still runs: with no local backend it falls back to the
scrapers, prints one `backend <name>: <reason>` line per attempt on stderr, and `wsc doctor`
reports `VERDICT DOWN` with a hint. Nothing else breaks. `fetch`, `pdf`, `map` and `crawl` never
used the local service in the first place.

## If the unit will not start

```bash
systemctl --user status searxng-local
journalctl --user -u searxng-local -n 40
```

The usual causes, in order of frequency:

- `python3.11` was missing at install time. Set `SEARX_PYTHON` to an interpreter you have and run
  `wsc setup --force` to rebuild the venv.
- The port is already taken. `ss -ltn | grep 8888` names the holder.
- A requirements bump left the venv stale. `wsc setup --force` recreates it from the pinned commit.

A rebuilt venv takes a few minutes, because it is a real pip install of SearXNG's requirements.
Nothing about that install is a Python dependency of `wsc`; the tool itself still has none.

`docs/install.md` is the installer page, which also covers the uninstall from the package side.

---

# docs/contributing.md

# Contributing

This repository has one rule about scope: it is a small, dependency-free, Linux-first CLI. A
change that adds a runtime dependency, a network call in a pure module, or a daemon does not
belong here. Everything else is open.

## Repo layout

The Python package is small on purpose. Each module owns one question, and the boundary between
them is the design.

| module | what it owns |
|---|---|
| `webscour/extract.py` | bytes to text. The HTML tokenizer, the search-result parsers, the sitemap and robots readers, the js-shell heuristic, the document router and the link filter. It defines the four decisions a caller makes on a result (`js_shell_reason`, `document_backend`, `filter_links`, `same_origin`) as pure functions, so the self-test and the unit tests check them with no network and no browser |
| `webscour/backends.py` | everything that talks to the network, plus the pacing. HTTP, the SearXNG client and its start-if-stopped path, the scraper fallbacks, the API clients for GitHub, Stack Exchange, Hacker News, arXiv and Discourse, the bot-check detector, and the render engines behind lightpanda and playwright |
| `webscour/sources.py` | the keyless single-purpose endpoints and their parsers. Each source is a pure parser plus the one request that feeds it, in that order, so a parser is testable without a socket |
| `webscour/routes.py` | URL to a structured endpoint, when a site publishes one. A route returns markdown or text, never HTML, and a route that declines is a fallback rather than an error |
| `webscour/cache.py` | the on-disk cache under `./.webscour/`: one file per fetched URL, an index beside them, a TTL and a prune |
| `webscour/cli.py` | the argv surface: verbs, flags, printing, exit codes. Every command parses its arguments, calls into the modules above, and decides what the user sees. It opens no socket itself |
| `webscour/argv.py` | the one place a JSON tool call becomes a command line. The MCP server and the pi extension both call it, so a flag is added once |
| `webscour/searx.py` | the search-backend lifecycle: install it, measure it, check it. It shells out to the scripts in `searx/` rather than reimplementing them, because those scripts are the ones a user can read and run by hand |
| `webscour/render_venv.py` | the optional playwright fallback and the venv this tool owns. One place is allowed to install a Python package, and this is it |
| `searx/` | the bundled SearXNG installer, the engine probe and the query-redacting WSGI entrypoint. Data shipped for a human to read and run, not a package module: it is not installed, not imported, and deliberately not linted |
| `mcp/` and `extensions/pi/` | the two front ends. Both are thin and both route through `webscour/argv.py` |

`tests/` holds the unit tests, the markdown conformance suite and the extraction benchmark,
`scripts/` holds the release gate, `docs/decisions/` holds the reasoning, and `skill/` holds the
agent-facing instructions that ship as a pi package and a Claude Code plugin.

## The `extract.py` rule

**`webscour/extract.py` must import no network module.** Not `socket`, not `ssl`, not
`http.client`, not `urllib.request`. It may parse `urllib.parse`, because that is string handling,
and it may shell out to a *local* binary (`pdftotext`, `pandoc`, `markitdown`), because reading a
file you already have is not a network operation.

The rule is enforced, not documented and hoped for. `tests/test_extract.py` installs an import
hook that raises `ImportError` for `socket`, `ssl` and `http`, imports the module in a subprocess,
and fails if the import does not survive. If you break the rule, the test names the module you
added.

The reason is testability: the extraction rules are the part most likely to be wrong, and they are
the part that must be checkable with no network, no SearXNG and no render backend. A module that
cannot open a socket cannot accidentally become an integration test. `webscour/sources.py` follows
the same split for the same reason: a parser takes a dict or an XML string, and the request lives
in its own function.

## Run the tests

```bash
python3 -m unittest discover -s tests
```

The suite is offline by construction. The fetch tests inject a fake `http_raw` and a fake
`render_page`, so no test reaches the network. Run a single file or a single class the ordinary
way:

```bash
python3 -m unittest tests.test_extract
python3 -m unittest tests.test_cli.ExitCodeTest
```

The offline self-test is a second, shipping gate over the same pure functions:

```bash
python3 -m webscour --self-test
```

It prints one `PASS <name>` line per check and a `SUMMARY pass=N fail=N` line, and exits non-zero
if anything failed. It runs in an installed package too, which is why it exists next to the unit
tests rather than instead of them.

## Run the release gate

```bash
./scripts/check.sh
```

That is the only definition of "releasable". It prints one `PASS <name>` or `FAIL <name> :: <why>`
line per check and a summary, and stops at the first failure. In order: `ruff check .`,
`ruff format --check .`, the unit tests, `--self-test`, the entry point, the tag agreement, the
build, `twine check`, then a set of guards.

The guards are the interesting part, because each one is a fact that has been wrong before:

- one version, in one place: `webscour.__version__` is the source, and the tag and the pi manifest
  must agree with it.
- text hygiene: no em dash, no en dash and no emoji in the prose we wrote. Fenced blocks are
  exempt on purpose, because a real capture is evidence and transpiling it would be a lie.
- the licence is present and is MIT, and the metadata says so.
- zero runtime dependencies, and no import could smuggle one in. Every module is parsed and its
  imports are checked against `sys.stdlib_module_names`.
- no shipped file names a home directory.
- the wheel holds the package and the `searx/` data files, and nothing else.
- every config file parses.

The script needs `ruff`, `build` and `twine` importable. The documented way to provide them is a
throwaway venv the gate itself does not create:

```bash
python3 -m venv .venv-dev && .venv-dev/bin/pip install ruff build twine
./scripts/check.sh
```

`.github/workflows/` are thin wrappers that install the same three tools and run the same script.
No check exists only in CI: if a workflow learns something `check.sh` does not know, the knowledge
belongs in the script.

## The extraction benchmark

`scripts/check.sh` runs offline, so the benchmark is not part of it. Set `BENCH=1` to add it, or
run it directly:

```bash
python3 tests/bench_extract.py                   # offline, from the captured fixtures
python3 tests/bench_extract.py --live            # re-fetch the pages first, then measure
python3 tests/bench_extract.py --tolerance 0.10  # allowed regression over the baseline
python3 tests/bench_extract.py --save-baseline tests/baselines/0.2.0.json
```

It compares our reading text with trafilatura's on six reference pages, from captured fixtures in
`tests/fixtures/bench/`, and fails when a page regresses past `tests/baselines/` or loses one of
its required phrases. Three numbers per page: bytes produced, lines produced, and `prec`, the
ratio of bytes out to bytes of naive visible text. A tolerance of 0.10 is the default.

trafilatura is measured, never depended on. It lives in a throwaway venv:

```bash
python3 -m venv /tmp/tfvenv && /tmp/tfvenv/bin/pip install trafilatura
```

When that venv is absent the trafilatura column reads `n/a` and only our own baseline decides.
That is deliberate: a benchmark that cannot run must not block a release, but it must be visible
in the output that it did not run.

A baseline is a file, not a claim. When a change is meant to improve extraction, save a new
baseline in the same commit and say in the message what moved.

## Decision records

**Every design choice that cost someone an argument gets a record in `docs/decisions/`.** The
form is fixed, because a record that varies in shape is a record nobody rereads:

- a numbered file name and a title: `0006 - <the decision in one line>`
- `**Status:**` with the date, so a reversal is visible
- `## Context`, `## Options`, `## Choice`, `## Evidence`, `## Reversal condition`

`## Evidence` is the part that separates this from an opinion: a measurement, a date, and the
command that produced it. `## Reversal condition` is the part that keeps a record honest: the
observation that would make you choose differently. A record without both is a press release.

The five records that exist cover: no Python dependencies, lightpanda required with playwright as
a fallback, the extraction tag list adapted from trafilatura's measured settings, silent stderr
with `-v`, and the playwright venv owned by the tool. Read them before you change the thing they
describe; if you disagree, write `0006` rather than editing `0003`.

## Commits

Conventional Commits, one logical change per commit.

```text
feat: add a --format markdown pass to wsc pdf
fix: keep a lone <pre> block verbatim when trimming whitespace
docs: state the loopback bind in the self-hosting page
```

While the major version is 0 there is no stable API to break, so the bump rules are flat:

| commit | bump |
|---|---|
| `fix:` | patch, `0.1.0` to `0.1.1` |
| `feat:` | minor, `0.1.0` to `0.2.0` |
| `perf:`, `refactor:`, `chore:`, `ci:` | patch |
| anything with `!` | minor while the major is 0 |
| anything with `!` | major at `1.0.0` and after |

That last pair is the whole point of `cliff.toml`. A 0.x project that jumps to `1.0.0` because
someone marked a commit breaking has lied to every user who reads the version as "same major, safe
to upgrade". Breaking changes become `1.0.0` when the maintainers say so, not when a commit
message says so.

Grouping into the changelog follows the same file: `feat` goes to Added, `fix` to Fixed, `perf`,
`refactor`, `chore` and `ci` to Changed, `docs` to Documentation, and `test` and `style` are
skipped. A hand-written `## Unreleased` section at the top of `CHANGELOG.md` is for notes no commit
message can carry.

## Cutting a release

```bash
./scripts/release.sh 0.2.0 --dry-run   # show what would happen
./scripts/release.sh 0.2.0             # gate, stamp, changelog, tag, print the push commands
```

The script refuses a dirty tree and a version that does not increase, runs `check.sh`, writes the
version into `webscour/__init__.py` and the pi manifest, builds the changelog section from git
cliff, commits and tags. It never pushes and never publishes: it prints those two commands so the
person running them has read them first. A pushed tag is published to the world, and a published
release cannot be withdrawn. `docs/maintaining.md` is the fuller runbook.

## Style

`ruff` decides formatting and linting, with `target-version = "py311"`, `line-length = 100`, and
sorted imports. Prose is wrapped by hand at roughly 100 columns and the formatter is told to leave
docstrings alone. Two conventions that are not ruff's business:

- **Stdout is the answer, stderr is the diagnostic.** A new line that explains a choice goes
  through `vwarn` and therefore behind `-v`. A lost capability goes through `warn` and always
  prints. A fact about the answer (`render:`, `route:`, `cache: hit`) is its own short exception
  and is documented where the verb is.
- **Report what you cannot confirm.** A docstring or a doc line that states a number should say
  where the number came from, and a fact you did not verify belongs in the report, not in the
  prose.
